nodes.label: Akkad and the Third Dynasty of Ur
nodes.full: The fallen empire this folio grows out of — Ur III's command economy, its Sumerian literary Renaissance, its Code of Ur-Namma, and the Amorite migration and southern salt that broke it. See mesopotamia-2334bc-2004bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio mesopotamia-2334bc-2004bc.

nodes.label: Kassite Babylonia
nodes.full: The dynasty of Kassite mountain people who take the Babylonian throne after the Hittite raid and hold the south, in stability, for four hundred years. See babylon-1595bc-1155bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio babylon-1595bc-1155bc.

nodes.label: The Hittite Kingdom
nodes.full: The Anatolian power that under Mursili I destroyed Aleppo and then raided down the Euphrates to sack Babylon around 1595, ending the First Dynasty.
nodes.src: background — Trevor Bryce, 'The Kingdom of the Hittites' (2005).

nodes.label: Elam of the Sukkalmah
nodes.full: Susa and Anshan under the 'Grand Regent' dynasty — a great power that overlorded the Amorite kings, organised the coalition Hammurabi broke, and shared the tin trade.
nodes.src: background — Daniel Potts, 'The Archaeology of Elam' (1999).

nodes.label: Anatolia and the caravan trade
nodes.full: The Anatolian kingdoms whose cities hosted the Assyrian trading colonies, took Babylonian and Assur textiles and eastern tin, and paid in silver and gold — and from which the horse and light chariot reached Mesopotamia.
nodes.src: background — Larsen, 'Ancient Kanesh' (2015).

nodes.label: Isin inherits the kingship of Ur
nodes.full: Ishbi-Erra, the officer who had broken away from Ibbi-Sin, founded a dynasty at Isin that held Nippur and claimed to have taken up the fallen kingship of Ur. Its kings kept the Sumerian royal-hymn tradition alive, issued a law collection under Lipit-Ishtar, and dominated the south for a century — until Larsa overtook them and Rim-Sin captured the city in 1794.
nodes.src: Douglas Frayne, RIME 4: 'Old Babylonian Period' (1990); Dietz Otto Edzard, 'Die "zweite Zwischenzeit" Babyloniens' (1957).

nodes.label: Larsa takes the lead in the south
nodes.full: Under Gungunum, Larsa wrested Ur from Isin in 1927 and campaigned into Elam, and over the next century it displaced Isin as the strongest southern kingdom. Larsa's wealth came from the date gardens and wool of the deep south and from the sun-god Shamash's great temple, the Ebabbar, whose archives document the shift of the region's centre of gravity away from Nippur.
nodes.src: Frayne, RIME 4 (1990); the Larsa economy in Marc Van De Mieroop, 'Society and Enterprise in Old Babylonian Ur' (1992).

nodes.label: Kudur-Mabuk's line and the long reign of Rim-Sin
nodes.full: The Elamite chief Kudur-Mabuk set his sons over Larsa — first Warad-Sin, then Rim-Sin I, who reigned some sixty years. Rim-Sin conquered Isin in 1794 and was so proud of it that he dated his regnal years by that conquest for the next thirty. He ruled the whole south from the Gulf to Nippur, and was one of the two most powerful kings in the land, until Hammurabi defeated and deposed him in 1763.
nodes.src: Marc Van De Mieroop, 'The Reign of Rim-Sin' (RA 1993); Frayne, RIME 4 (1990).

nodes.label: Shamshi-Adad's Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia
nodes.full: An Amorite from the Ekallatum line, Shamshi-Adad seized Assur, then Mari, then the whole northern Jazira, and ruled it from a rebuilt capital, Shubat-Enlil, delegating Ekallatum to his capable son Ishme-Dagan and Mari to his idle son Yasmah-Addu. It was the first territorial state to unite the north — and it broke apart within a year of his death.
nodes.src: Dominique Charpin & Nele Ziegler, 'Mari et le Proche-Orient à l'époque amorrite' (2003); the Shamshi-Adad correspondence in the Mari archives.

nodes.label: Zimri-Lim of Mari and the great palace
nodes.full: After Shamshi-Adad's death the old Lim dynasty returned to Mari in the person of Zimri-Lim, who held the middle Euphrates, married a daughter of Yarim-Lim of Aleppo, and kept a court whose sprawling palace and archive of more than twenty thousand letters and records is the richest window we have on the age. His ally Hammurabi captured Mari in 1761 and levelled it two years later.
nodes.src: Jean-Marie Durand, 'Les documents épistolaires du palais de Mari' I–III (1997–2000); Wolfgang Heimpel, 'Letters to the King of Mari' (2003).

nodes.label: The merchant city-state of Assur
nodes.full: Except for the interval under Shamshi-Adad, Assur was a small oligarchic city-state on the Tigris governed jointly by a hereditary 'steward', an official who gave his name to the year, and an assembly known simply as 'the City'. It had little land and no army worth the name; its entire wealth came from running the caravan trade to Anatolia.
nodes.src: Klaas Veenhof & Jesper Eidem, 'Mesopotamia: The Old Assyrian Period' (OBO 160/5, 2008); Mogens Trolle Larsen, 'The Old Assyrian City-State and its Colonies' (1976).

nodes.label: The First Dynasty builds Babylon
nodes.full: Five Amorite kings from Sumu-abum to Sin-muballit turned Babylon from an obscure town into a middling kingdom of northern Babylonia — Sippar, Kish, Borsippa, Dilbat — walling the city, digging canals, and fighting Larsa, Isin and Eshnunna for room. It was a modest inheritance, and it is the base from which Hammurabi built an empire.
nodes.src: Frayne, RIME 4 (1990); Marc Van De Mieroop, 'King Hammurabi of Babylon: A Biography' (2005), ch. 1.

nodes.label: Hammurabi of Babylon
nodes.full: For most of his forty-three years Hammurabi was one strong king among several — a Mari report ranks him level with Rim-Sin of Larsa and Ibal-pi-El of Eshnunna, each with ten or fifteen lesser kings 'following' him. Then from 1764 he moved fast: he broke an Elamite-led coalition, took Larsa, crushed Eshnunna, destroyed his ally Mari, and subdued Assyria, ruling all Mesopotamia by 1755. His year-names and his law stele record it.
nodes.src: Marc Van De Mieroop, 'King Hammurabi of Babylon' (2005); Dominique Charpin, 'Hammurabi of Babylon' (2012); the 'ten kings' letter is Mari text ARM VI 27.

nodes.label: Samsu-iluna and the loss of the south
nodes.full: Hammurabi's son inherited the empire and immediately faced a vast revolt — a pretender styling himself Rim-Sin II, joined by Eshnunna, the southern cities and the Kassites. He held the north but lost the south for good: Ur, Uruk, Larsa and Nippur were abandoned around 1740, their archives falling silent, and a 'Sealand' dynasty took the marshes. Babylon contracted to its home region.
nodes.src: Frayne, RIME 4 (1990); Seth Richardson, 'The Collapse of a Complex State: A Reappraisal of the End of the First Dynasty of Babylon' (2002).

nodes.label: The late kings and the Venus tablet
nodes.full: Abi-eshuh, Ammi-ditana, Ammi-saduqa and their successors ruled a shrunken kingdom of northern Babylonia — consolidating, digging canals, repeatedly cancelling debts by decree, and absorbing Kassite groups as soldiers and workers. Ammi-saduqa's reign produced the tablet of Venus observations that anchors the whole disputed chronology of the Bronze Age.
nodes.src: Frayne, RIME 4 (1990); Erica Reiner & David Pingree, 'The Venus Tablet of Ammiṣaduqa' (1975).

nodes.label: Samsu-ditana and the Hittite sack
nodes.full: The last king of the dynasty ruled thirty years over the diminished kingdom, and then, around 1595, the Hittite king Mursili I struck down the Euphrates in a raid of unheard-of range, sacked Babylon, and carried off the statues of Marduk and his consort. The dynasty ended. After a murky interval, the Kassites — long resident in the land — took the throne.
nodes.src: The Hittite 'Edict of Telipinu' and the 'Chronicle of Early Kings'; Trevor Bryce, 'The Kingdom of the Hittites' (2005).

nodes.label: The kings who called each other brother
nodes.full: The Mari letters show an international system: a dozen Amorite kingdoms from the Zagros to the Mediterranean whose rulers addressed one another as 'brother' among equals or 'father' and 'son' by rank, sent resident envoys, sealed treaties by touching the throat and swearing by the gods, married across borders, and shared pastoral tribes whose loyalties crossed every frontier. It is the earliest well-documented diplomacy of the ancient world.
nodes.src: Jean-Marie Durand, 'La diplomatie mésopotamienne'; Bertrand Lafont, 'Relations internationales, alliances et diplomatie au temps des rois de Mari' (2001).

nodes.label: Isin against Larsa
nodes.full: For well over a century Isin and Larsa fought a war of attrition over the south — for Ur, for the sun-temple at Larsa, and above all for control of Nippur, whose god Enlil conferred legitimate kingship over the land. Nippur changed hands repeatedly, kings dated their years by its capture, and the contest ended only when Rim-Sin of Larsa took Isin itself in 1794.
nodes.src: Reconstructed from year-names and inscriptions in Frayne, RIME 4 (1990); D. O. Edzard (1957).

nodes.label: The shifting coalitions of the 1770s
nodes.full: The Mari archive captures a decade of fluid, multi-sided war: Babylon, Larsa, Eshnunna, Elam as would-be overlord, Mari, Aleppo, Qatna and the mountain Turukkeans forming and breaking alliances season by season. One much-quoted report tells the king of Mari that no ruler is strong alone — 'ten or fifteen kings follow Hammurabi, as many follow Rim-Sin, as many Ibal-pi-El of Eshnunna.'
nodes.src: Mari text ARM VI 27 and the wider correspondence; Wolfgang Heimpel, 'Letters to the King of Mari' (2003).

nodes.label: The conquest of Mesopotamia, 1764–1755
nodes.full: In his thirtieth year Hammurabi shattered a coalition led by Elam; in his thirty-first he conquered Rim-Sin's Larsa and the whole south; in his thirty-second he beat Eshnunna, the Gutians and Subartu; then he took Mari, and finally reduced Assyria. In little more than a decade a mid-sized kingdom became the master of Mesopotamia — a transformation his own year-names narrate step by step.
nodes.src: Hammurabi's year-names 30–38 in Frayne, RIME 4 (1990); Charpin, 'Hammurabi of Babylon' (2012).

nodes.label: The destruction of Mari
nodes.full: Hammurabi took Mari from his former ally Zimri-Lim in 1761, garrisoned it, and two years later pulled down its walls and set fire to the great palace. The fire baked and buried the twenty-thousand-tablet archive where it lay. Mari's ruin was a strategic act; its unintended result was to preserve the fullest record of Amorite Mesopotamia for the excavators of the 1930s.
nodes.src: André Parrot's Mari excavations; the destruction in Charpin & Ziegler (2003) and Durand's archive editions.

nodes.label: The great revolt and the abandonment of Sumer
nodes.full: A coalition rising in Samsu-iluna's tenth year — a pretender, Eshnunna, the southern cities and the Kassites — was beaten in the north but won in the south. Within a decade the old Sumerian cities were emptying: temple archives break off, canals silted, the population drained toward the north or into the marshes, where a 'Sealand' dynasty held out. The heartland of Sumer, urban for two thousand years, was largely abandoned for the next several centuries.
nodes.src: Seth Richardson, 'The Collapse of a Complex State' (2002); the settlement evidence in Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981).

nodes.label: The Hittite raid on Babylon
nodes.full: The Hittite king Mursili I, having destroyed Aleppo, drove on down the Euphrates in a strike of unprecedented reach, took Babylon, plundered it, and carried the statues of Marduk and Sarpanitu back toward Anatolia (they were later recovered from Hana). He did not stay — but the First Dynasty was finished, and after a gap of uncertain length the Kassites ruled Babylon.
nodes.src: The Hittite 'Edict of Telipinu' and the Babylonian 'Chronicle of Early Kings'; Bryce, 'The Kingdom of the Hittites' (2005).

nodes.label: The Code of Hammurabi
nodes.full: A two-metre pillar of black diorite, topped by a relief of Hammurabi standing before the enthroned sun-god to receive the emblems of rule, and covered with some 282 rulings on theft, land, loans, marriage, inheritance, assault, and the malpractice of doctors and builders, between a prologue of royal piety and an epilogue of blessings and curses. No court is known to have cited it. It is a monument to the king as the source of justice, and the fullest single picture of a Bronze Age society's rules.
nodes.src: Martha Roth, 'Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor' (1997), pp. 71–142; Jean Bottéro, 'The "Code" of Hammurabi' (1992).

nodes.label: The talion and the three classes
nodes.full: 'If a man blinds the eye of another man, they shall blind his eye' — but only if the victim is an awilum, a free man of standing. Blind a mushkenum, a commoner or dependent, and you pay a mina of silver; blind a man's slave, and you pay half the slave's value to its owner. Retribution in kind, and the graded worth of a person by rank, are the two ideas around which the Code is built.
nodes.src: Roth (1997), laws 196–214; the class terms discussed in Raymond Westbrook, 'Studies in Biblical and Cuneiform Law' (1988).

nodes.label: The codes before Hammurabi
nodes.full: Royal law-collections were an established genre before Hammurabi: the Laws of Ur-Namma, of Lipit-Ishtar of Isin, and of the kingdom of Eshnunna all survive, mostly settling injuries by payment rather than by retaliation. Hammurabi's stele is the largest, the best preserved, and the most self-glorifying — not the first. What it added was scale, the retributive principle, and a monument meant to last.
nodes.src: Roth (1997); Reuven Yaron, 'The Laws of Eshnunna' (2nd ed. 1988).

nodes.label: The mišarum edict — the clean slate
nodes.full: On accession and at intervals a Babylonian king proclaimed mišarum, 'equity': consumer debts and arrears were cancelled, people sold into debt-slavery and land pledged for loans were released, and some prices were reset. Ammi-saduqa's edict survives clause by clause. It was deliberate macroeconomic policy — periodically unwinding a build-up of private debt before it choked production and drove the indebted to flee or rebel.
nodes.src: Fritz Rudolf Kraus, 'Ein Edikt des Königs Ammi-ṣaduqa von Babylon' (1958) and 'Königliche Verfügungen in altbabylonischer Zeit' (1984).

nodes.label: The city assembly and commercial law of Assur
nodes.full: Assur was run by its assembly, 'the City', and its annually changing eponym, and it developed the earliest substantial body of commercial law: written partnership and agency contracts, the naruqqum joint fund pooling many investors' silver for a term of years, procedures for debt, arbitration and default, all enforced between the mother city and its trading colonies a thousand kilometres away.
nodes.src: Mogens Trolle Larsen, 'The Old Assyrian City-State and its Colonies' (1976); Klaas Veenhof, 'Aspects of Old Assyrian Trade and its Terminology' (1972).

nodes.label: The year-name, the archive and the private contract
nodes.full: Every document was dated by a 'year-name' commemorating a deed of the year before — 'the year Hammurabi destroyed the wall of Mari' — and king-lists strung these into chronology. And the enforceable instrument of private life was the sealed clay tablet, often shut inside an inscribed envelope: the loan, the sale, the marriage, the adoption. The archives of Sippar, Nippur, Ur and Larsa are the age's richest record precisely because ordinary people kept their papers.
nodes.src: Marc Van De Mieroop, 'Cuneiform Texts and the Writing of History' (1999); the Sippar archives in Rivkah Harris, 'Ancient Sippar' (1975).

nodes.label: Marduk of Babylon on the rise
nodes.full: At the start of the period Marduk was a minor deity, the local god of an unimportant town. As Babylon rose he rose with it: the prologue to Hammurabi's Code states that Anu and Enlil have handed Marduk 'the Enlil-power over all the people' and made Babylon supreme. The theological promotion that ends, a thousand years on, with Marduk creating the world in Enuma Elish begins in these lines.
nodes.src: W. G. Lambert, 'Babylonian Creation Myths' (2013); the Code prologue in Roth (1997).

nodes.label: The personal god and the righteous sufferer
nodes.full: Each Old Babylonian person had a personal god and goddess who stood between them and the great deities and carried their prayers up. Misfortune meant the personal god had turned away, usually for a sin the sufferer might not know. The Sumerian poem 'Man and His God' has a blameless man lament his undeserved affliction until his god relents — the first treatment of the problem that later produces the Book of Job and the 'Babylonian Theodicy'.
nodes.src: Thorkild Jacobsen, 'The Treasures of Darkness' (1976); 'Man and His God' in W. G. Lambert, 'Babylonian Wisdom Literature' (1960).

nodes.label: The naditu women of Sippar
nodes.full: Daughters of the Sippar elite were dedicated to the sun-god Shamash as naditu — living unmarried inside a walled cloister, forbidden children, but free to own and work property, lend silver at interest, buy and sell land, and adopt an heir, usually a niece who was herself a naditu. Hundreds of their tablets survive. It was a large, wealthy, self-renewing institution built around women's economic agency, with no real later parallel in Mesopotamia.
nodes.src: Rivkah Harris, 'Ancient Sippar: A Demographic Study of an Old-Babylonian City' (1975); Elizabeth Stone's work on the naditu of Nippur.

nodes.label: The prophets of Mari
nodes.full: Officials at Mari forwarded to King Zimri-Lim the unsolicited messages of prophets — the āpilum, the ecstatic muḫḫûm, and ordinary people reporting dreams — in which a god spoke directly: demanding a neglected offering, promising victory, or warning of a plot. Often a lock of the speaker's hair and a piece of their hem were sent with the report for verification. It is the earliest large body of Near Eastern prophecy, and strikingly like the prophets of the Hebrew Bible.
nodes.src: Martti Nissinen, 'Prophets and Prophecy in the Ancient Near East' (2003); the Mari letters in ARM XXVI/1 (Durand 1988).

nodes.label: The kispum and the royal ancestors
nodes.full: Beside the temple round — the akitu, the monthly offerings, Hammurabi's boasted temple-building — ran the cult of the dead. Each month the reigning king held the kispum, a funerary meal at which he 'fed' his named royal ancestors and the anonymous Amorite dead. A document known as the Genealogy of the Hammurabi Dynasty lists the ancestors he was obliged to remember, binding the living king to a deep and partly fictional line.
nodes.src: J. J. Finkelstein, 'The Genealogy of the Hammurabi Dynasty' (JCS 1966); the kispum ritual in Jack Sasson's studies.

nodes.label: The demon and the amulet
nodes.full: Under the ordered pantheon swarmed the hostile powers of the everyday: Lamashtu who snatched the newborn, the utukku that lurked in the dark, the restless ghost of the unburied. Against them people used incantation, the protective clay figurine sealed under the threshold, and amulets — the snarling head of the demon Pazuzu worn to frighten Lamashtu off. Much of lived religion was this daily, defensive counter-magic.
nodes.src: Frans Wiggermann, 'Lamaštu, Daughter of Anu' (2000); the Old Babylonian incantation corpus and apotropaic figurines.

nodes.label: The relief on the Code stele
nodes.full: At the top of the law pillar, carved in high relief, Hammurabi stands with one hand raised before the sun-god Shamash, who sits enthroned on a mountain, rays rising from his shoulders, holding out the rod and the coiled ring. The king is receiving justice from the god, to dispense to men. The style is deliberately grave and archaising, and the whole stele is shaped like a boundary-marker — a claim staked in stone.
nodes.src: Louvre (Sb 8); Zainab Bahrani, 'The Graven Image: Representation in Babylonia and Assyria' (2003).

nodes.label: Gilgamesh and Atra-hasis — Akkadian literature comes of age
nodes.full: The Old Babylonian period produced the first true literature in Akkadian: an early version of the Gilgamesh epic — 'surpassing all kings', the wild man Enkidu, the death-haunted friendship — and Atra-hasis, which tells how humans were made from clay to carry the gods' workload, multiplied until their noise disturbed the gods, and were nearly wiped out by a flood one man survived in a boat. The Genesis flood story descends from it.
nodes.src: Andrew George, 'The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic' (2003), the OB tablets; W. G. Lambert & A. R. Millard, 'Atra-ḫasīs' (1969); Benjamin Foster, 'Before the Muses' (2005).

nodes.label: The Sumerian classics in the schoolroom
nodes.full: Almost all the Sumerian literature we have — the hymns and myths, the debate poems, the Sumerian tales of Gilgamesh, the city laments — survives because Old Babylonian schoolboys at Nippur and elsewhere copied it as homework, over and over, in a fixed sequence. When the southern schools closed after 1740 that transmission narrowed sharply; much Sumerian literature is known from a single teaching town and a single generation.
nodes.src: Steve Tinney, 'On the Curricular Setting of Sumerian Literature' (Iraq 1999); Niek Veldhuis, 'Elementary Education at Nippur' (1997).

nodes.label: The terracotta plaque and the Queen of the Night
nodes.full: Cheap fired-clay reliefs pressed from moulds and sold in the market brought images into every house: gods and protective demons, a harpist, a couple on a bed, a woman at a window, a man with his dog. The finest surviving example is the large 'Queen of the Night' — a nude, winged, bird-taloned goddess between two owls and two lions, once brightly painted — probably a form of Ishtar for a shrine.
nodes.src: Elizabeth Douglas Van Buren, 'Clay Figurines of Babylonia and Assyria' (1930); Dominique Collon, 'The Queen of the Night' (2005).

nodes.label: The Old Babylonian presentation seal
nodes.full: The standard cylinder seal of the age shows a single scene: a worshipper led by a goddess with both hands raised in intercession — the 'suppliant goddess' — toward a seated king or deity, with minor figures and symbols filling the field, and a long inscription naming the owner, his father, and the god he serves. Rolled onto every contract, it was at once a legal signature and a compact statement of who a person was.
nodes.src: Dominique Collon, 'First Impressions: Cylinder Seals in the Ancient Near East' (1987); Lamia Al-Gailani Werr, 'Old Babylonian Cylinder Seals' (1988).

nodes.label: The earliest theory of music
nodes.full: A handful of cuneiform tablets name the nine strings of the Mesopotamian lyre, list seven diatonic tuning-sets, and give instructions for shifting from one to the next by tightening or loosening a single string — a cycle equivalent to moving through the keys by fifths. It is the oldest written account of an organised musical scale system found anywhere, four hundred years before the Hurrian hymn that these rules let scholars attempt to sing.
nodes.src: Anne Draffkorn Kilmer, 'The Discovery of an Ancient Mesopotamian Theory of Music' (1971); the tuning texts UET VII 74 and CBS 10996; Theo Krispijn's studies.

nodes.label: The golden age of Babylonian mathematics
nodes.full: Old Babylonian scribes did the most sophisticated mathematics anywhere before Greece: they solved quadratic and some cubic problems, computed a square root of two accurate to six sexagesimal places, drew up tables of what we call Pythagorean triples, and worked routine problems of area, volume, interest and labour — all in base-sixty place-value notation, as school exercises and as a working professional's toolkit.
nodes.src: Eleanor Robson, 'Mathematics in Ancient Iraq: A Social History' (2008), ch. 3–4; Jens Høyrup, 'Lengths, Widths, Surfaces' (2002); Robson, 'Words and Pictures: New Light on Plimpton 322' (2002).

nodes.label: The omen organised into a series
nodes.full: The diviner's practice was becoming a literature. The markings of the sacrificed liver, the movements of the heavens, malformed births, the behaviour of animals and oil on water were each being gathered into long, ordered compendia of 'if this is seen, then that will follow' — the ancestors of the great canonical series of the first millennium. Divination was treated as an empirical discipline with a growing reference library.
nodes.src: Ulla Koch, 'Secrets of Extispicy' (2005); Francesca Rochberg, 'Before Nature: Cuneiform Knowledge and the History of Science' (2016).

nodes.label: The Venus Tablet and dated observation
nodes.full: For twenty-one years of Ammi-saduqa's reign, observers recorded the dates on which Venus first appeared and disappeared as morning and evening star, and read omens from them. The list, preserved in a much later copy, is the earliest run of systematic dated celestial observation — and, because Venus's cycle repeats on a known schedule, the single most important peg for the whole disputed chronology of the Bronze Age Near East.
nodes.src: Erica Reiner & David Pingree, 'The Venus Tablet of Ammiṣaduqa' (1975); the chronology debate in Hermann Gasche et al., 'Dating the Fall of Babylon' (1998).

nodes.label: The fixed curriculum
nodes.full: By the Old Babylonian period the scribal school ran a set sequence — sign-lists, then vocabularies, then model contracts and mathematical tables, then proverbs, then a core of ten literary works — reproduced with little variation across the land. Grammatical texts analysed Sumerian systematically, and 'examination texts' and 'dialogues' dramatised the pupil's ordeal. A codified pedagogy now trained every literate person the same way.
nodes.src: Niek Veldhuis, 'Elementary Education at Nippur' (1997) and 'History of the Cuneiform Lexical Tradition' (2014).

nodes.label: The proverb and the counsel of experience
nodes.full: Alongside the certainties of the omen ran a sceptical, worldly tradition: collections of thousands of Sumerian proverbs copied in school, the still-current Instructions of Shuruppak, fable and satire, and poems worrying at why the just suffer. Mesopotamia held two ways of knowing the world at once — the diviner's rule-bound reading of signs, and the sharp, resigned common sense of the sayings.
nodes.src: Bendt Alster, 'Proverbs of Ancient Sumer' (1997); W. G. Lambert, 'Babylonian Wisdom Literature' (1960).

nodes.label: The private operator comes into his own
nodes.full: After Ur III's command economy, the Old Babylonian period is the age of the individual: land bought and sold freely, houses split among heirs, fields leased for a share of the crop, and above all the tamkārum — merchant, moneylender, investor — operating on his own account. The family archives of men like Balamunamhe of Larsa and the Ur-Utu household at Sippar show fortunes built outside the palace and the temple.
nodes.src: Norman Yoffee, 'The Economic Role of the Crown in the Old Babylonian Period' (1977); Marc Van De Mieroop, 'Society and Enterprise in Old Babylonian Ur' (1992).

nodes.label: The Assur–Kanesh donkey caravans
nodes.full: Assur ran a trade so specialised it left almost no trace of the goods and a mountain of paperwork. Firms bought tin brought from the east and textiles woven in Babylonia and Assur, loaded them on trains of black donkeys, and drove them a thousand kilometres over the Taurus to Kanesh in central Anatolia, where they sold for silver and gold at a markup of half or more. Some twenty-three thousand of their letters and accounts survive from Kültepe.
nodes.src: Klaas Veenhof & Jesper Eidem, 'Mesopotamia: The Old Assyrian Period' (2008); Mogens Trolle Larsen, 'Ancient Kanesh: A Merchant Colony in Bronze Age Anatolia' (2015).

nodes.label: Land held for service — the ilkum
nodes.full: A large part of the farmland was held on ilkum tenure: the state assigned a field to a soldier, an official or a craftsman, who worked it and drew its produce in exchange for owing the crown military service or labour. The Code protects the absent soldier's ilkum field from seizure and forbids its sale. Much of the agrarian economy thus ran not on rent or wages but on this standing exchange of land for duty.
nodes.src: Code of Hammurabi, laws 26–41 (Roth 1997); F. R. Kraus, 'Vom mesopotamischen Menschen der altbabylonischen Zeit' (1973).

nodes.label: Larsa's last prosperous generation
nodes.full: Before the abandonment, the deep south was still rich: the date gardens and wool of Larsa, the estates of the sun-temple, the fisheries of the marshes, and the Ur merchants who still sailed to Dilmun for copper. The Rim-Sin and early Hammurabi archives from Ur and Larsa show a dense, monetised rural economy — the final chapter of a farmed landscape three thousand years old.
nodes.src: Marc Van De Mieroop, 'Society and Enterprise in Old Babylonian Ur' (1992); the Larsa archives in D. Charpin, 'Le clergé d'Ur au siècle d'Hammurabi' (1986).

nodes.label: The emptying of the oldest farmland
nodes.full: The south failed for several reasons at once: the Euphrates shifted its main channel west, away from Nippur and Isin; salt kept rising in the fields; two decades of revolt and reconquest drained the population; and in the 1740 campaigns the Babylonians deliberately breached southern canals. The result was that the alluvial heartland of Sumer, continuously farmed and cities since the Ubaid, was largely deserted for the next three or four centuries.
nodes.src: Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981); Hermann Gasche and the Euphrates-channel evidence; Seth Richardson (2002).

nodes.label: Silver, weight and the managed price
nodes.full: There was no coin, but the economy was monetised: silver by weight — the shekel and the mina — was the universal measure of value and the usual means of large payment. The Code and the mišarum edicts publish reference figures — a hired man's yearly wage, the rent of an ox or a boat, a surgeon's fee, the maximum interest — the state's attempt to hold a price level in a market it did not control.
nodes.src: Code of Hammurabi, laws 215–277 (Roth 1997); price and wage data in Karl Butz and in the Ammi-saduqa edict (Kraus 1958).

nodes.label: The arch and vault in routine use
nodes.full: Old Babylonian builders used the radiating brick arch for city gates and drains and barrel-vaulting for storerooms and tomb chambers as a matter of course — still in mud and baked brick set in bitumen or gypsum mortar, without the refinements of Roman masonry, but applied confidently wherever a span was needed in a land without long timber.
nodes.src: Building technique in Peter Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994); OB arched gates at Ur and elsewhere (Woolley).

nodes.label: The first true glass
nodes.full: Small beads and inlays of true glass — sand, plant ash and lime fused to a coloured, non-crystalline solid, distinct from the older glazed faience — appear in this period, probably as a by-product of the metal and faience workshops. It is still rare and precious. Within a century or two glass would be an industry in its own right, and the first written recipes for making it would be compiled.
nodes.src: Peter Moorey, 'Ancient Mesopotamian Materials and Industries' (1994); Robert Brill's compositional studies of early Mesopotamian glass.

nodes.label: The water-clock
nodes.full: To divide the day and night into watches for temple service, guard duty and astronomical observation, Babylonians used the water-clock — a vessel that drained or filled at a steady rate, its markings read off as time. Old Babylonian texts tabulate the weight of water for each month, adjusting for the fact that the night is longer in winter: a working, calibrated instrument for measuring elapsed time.
nodes.src: David Brown, John Fermor & Christopher Walker, 'The Water Clock in Mesopotamia' (AfO 1999–2000); the monthly water-weight tables in Enuma Anu Enlil Tablet 14.

nodes.label: The horse and the light chariot arrive
nodes.full: By the end of the period the true horse — larger and faster than the onager hybrids of the third millennium — and the light, spoked-wheel chariot had reached Mesopotamia from the steppe by way of Anatolia and the Zagros. The Mari letters mention horses as costly gifts and prestige mounts. The battlefield revolution they would bring — the chariot army, the horse as an arm of state — belongs to the centuries that follow.
nodes.src: Mary Littauer & Joost Crouwel, 'Wheeled Vehicles and Ridden Animals in the Ancient Near East' (1979); horse references in the Mari archives (Durand).

nodes.label: The karum — the extraterritorial colony
nodes.full: An Assyrian merchant colony sat beside the Anatolian city it served as a karum — a 'quay' or 'port' — a walled quarter of resident traders governed by their own assembly and courts, under a written treaty with the local king that guaranteed their safety, fixed the tolls and taxes on their goods, and promised compensation for losses. It is a network of self-governing trade enclaves two and a half thousand years before the medieval merchant colony.
nodes.src: Mogens Trolle Larsen, 'The Old Assyrian City-State and its Colonies' (1976); the Kanesh treaties in Klaas Veenhof, 'The Old Assyrian List of Year Eponyms' and 'Old Assyrian Trade' (2008).

nodes.label: The tin route
nodes.full: Tin, essential for bronze and mined nowhere near Mesopotamia, moved west from sources on the Iranian plateau — and probably from as far as Afghanistan — through Susa and Eshnunna to Assur and Mari, and on toward the Mediterranean via Aleppo. The Mari archives record consignments of tin sent west, some destined for Crete. Every kingdom on the route taxed it, and control of the flow was a matter of state.
nodes.src: The Mari tin texts (Georges Dossin; Jack Sasson); Guillaume Gernez on Bronze Age metal supply; Daniel Potts, 'Mesopotamian Civilization' (1997).

nodes.label: The states-system of the Mari letters
nodes.full: The Mari archive documents a working international order: permanent envoys at foreign courts, treaties sworn 'by the throat' and on the symbols of the gods, dynastic marriages used as alliances, the extradition of fugitives, formal declarations of 'brotherhood' or subordination, and a shared etiquette of gifts and correspondence. It is the fullest picture of ancient diplomacy before the Amarna letters three centuries later.
nodes.src: Bertrand Lafont, 'Relations internationales, alliances et diplomatie au temps des rois de Mari' (2001); Wolfgang Heimpel, 'Letters to the King of Mari' (2003).

nodes.label: Ea-nasir and the copper of Dilmun
nodes.full: Ur merchants still sailed to Dilmun for Magan copper in Hammurabi's day. One of them, Ea-nasir, is remembered for a tablet on which a furious customer named Nanni complains that the copper delivered was poor quality, that his messengers were sent back empty-handed 'through enemy territory', and that he had been treated with contempt. It is the oldest written customer complaint that survives.
nodes.src: The complaint tablet UET V 81 (British Museum BM 131236); A. Leo Oppenheim, 'Letters from Mesopotamia' (1967), no. 68.

nodes.label: Elam of the Sukkalmah
nodes.full: Elam under its 'Grand Regent' (sukkalmah) dynasty was a great power the Mesopotamian kings had to reckon with — an overlord the Mari rulers courted as 'father', the organiser of the coalition Hammurabi broke in 1764, a partner and rival in the tin trade. And it was Elam that, centuries on, would carry off the Code stele and Naram-Sin's Victory Stele as plunder to Susa, where the archaeologists found them.
nodes.src: Daniel Potts, 'The Archaeology of Elam' (1999), ch. 5; the sukkalmah in the Mari correspondence (Charpin & Ziegler 2003).

nodes.label: The Amorite connective culture
nodes.full: A shared West-Semitic elite now ran the whole region — Babylon, Larsa, Mari, Aleppo, Qatna, Assur, Eshnunna all under Amorite dynasties — with common personal names, a common set of tribal categories (Sim'al and Yamina), the same god Dagan and cult of the ancestral tomb, and the same language of royal 'brotherhood'. The Amorites were less an invasion than the medium through which goods, people and ideas now moved across the Fertile Crescent.
nodes.src: Daniel Fleming, 'Democracy's Ancient Ancestors: Mari and Early Collective Governance' (2004); Aaron Burke, 'The Amorites and the Bronze Age Near East' (2021).

nodes.label: The Amorite settlement completed
nodes.full: By the eighteenth century every dynasty from the Zagros to the Mediterranean was Amorite, and their kingdoms carried a double structure: a king who was also the head of a tribal confederation, walled cities alongside tent-camps of the same people, and a political vocabulary that mixed the vocabulary of kingship with that of the sheikh and the clan. It was a lasting fusion of settled monarchy and pastoral confederacy.
nodes.src: Daniel Fleming, 'Democracy's Ancient Ancestors: Mari and Early Collective Governance' (2004).

nodes.label: The centre of gravity moves north
nodes.full: With the old Sumerian cities of the far south abandoned after 1740, 'Babylonia' came to mean the northern alluvium — Babylon, Sippar, Kish, Kutha, Borsippa — where the Euphrates still ran full and the land was less salted. The southward pull that had defined Mesopotamian civilisation for three thousand years reversed for good. The stage on which the later Babylonian and Assyrian kingdoms would contend was now set in the middle and the north.
nodes.src: Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981); the demographic reversal in Seth Richardson (2002).

nodes.label: Akkadian the vernacular, Sumerian the school tongue
nodes.full: By now Babylonian Akkadian was what people spoke, wrote letters in, and drew up contracts in. Sumerian had become a learned language — the medium of school, liturgy and high culture, mastered only by scribes, and increasingly translated line-by-line into Akkadian for teaching. This split between a living vernacular and a prestigious dead classical language would last as long as cuneiform itself.
nodes.src: Jerrold Cooper, 'Sumerian and Akkadian' (1996); the bilingual teaching texts in Niek Veldhuis (2014).

nodes.label: A drier age and the wandering rivers
nodes.full: The early and middle second millennium was a drier phase in Mesopotamia, and the rivers moved: the Euphrates shifted its principal channel westward, leaving Nippur, Isin and Adab on failing branches while the western line through Babylon and Sippar stayed strong. Climate and hydrology were not the background to the century's upheavals — they were among its causes.
nodes.src: Hermann Gasche et al. on Euphrates channel change; palaeoclimate synthesis in Arie Issar & Mattanyah Zohar, 'Climate Change: Environment and History of the Near East' (2004).

nodes.label: The schoolboy of the eduba
nodes.full: The Sumerian 'Schooldays' text follows a pupil through his day: up before dawn, a lunch of two rolls, the walk to the tablet house, and a stream of canings — for lateness, for talking, for a badly formed sign, for standing up without leave, for speaking Sumerian with an accent. His father ends the story by feasting and bribing the teacher, who then praises the boy. It is half complaint, half advertisement for the school's discipline.
nodes.src: Samuel Noah Kramer, 'Schooldays: A Sumerian Composition Relating to the Education of a Scribe' (JAOS 1949); Herman Vanstiphout's studies of the 'eduba' texts.

nodes.label: The three ranks of the Code
nodes.full: The Code sorts people into three: the awilum, the full free citizen; the mushkenum, a dependent or commoner of lower standing — better protected than a slave but cheaper to injure, and himself liable to lighter penalties; and the wardum, the slave, who is property with a few protections. Which real people the elusive middle term, mushkenum, actually covered — palace dependants, the free poor, both — has been argued for a century.
nodes.src: Code of Hammurabi (Roth 1997); the mushkenum debate reviewed in Raymond Westbrook (ed.), 'A History of Ancient Near Eastern Law' (2003).

nodes.label: The merchant's wife in Assur
nodes.full: With the men away in Anatolia for years at a stretch, the women of the Assur trading families ran the home end of the business: raising the children, managing the creditors and the household, and above all weaving — and dispatching by caravan — the textiles that were the firm's own product. The letters of women like Lamassi and Tarām-Kūbi to absent husbands mix accounts, reproach and worry, and are among the most vivid personal documents of the age.
nodes.src: Cécile Michel, 'Women of Assur and Kanesh' (2020); the letters in Michel, 'Correspondance des marchands de Kaniš' (2001).

nodes.label: The debtor and the clean slate
nodes.full: A free man with a small field, a bad harvest, and a loan at a third interest could within a year pledge his ox, then his land, then his wife or son, then himself. The Code caps such debt-service at three years; the mišarum edict wiped the slate clean every decade or so. In between, the slide from free smallholder to bondsman was one of the commonest trajectories a life could take.
nodes.src: Code of Hammurabi, laws 115–119, 151–152 (Roth 1997); the debt cycle in F. R. Kraus, 'Königliche Verfügungen in altbabylonischer Zeit' (1984).

nodes.label: The soldier and his field
nodes.full: The redum and bairum — the king's soldiers — held a field, a house and a garden from the crown in return for going on campaign and turning out for the canal work. The Code protects that land while he is away, forbids his officers to hire a substitute in his place, and lays a duty on his city or temple to ransom him if he is captured. War, land tenure and citizenship were bound together in one obligation.
nodes.src: Code of Hammurabi, laws 26–41 (Roth 1997); the ilkum soldier in F. R. Kraus, 'Vom mesopotamischen Menschen' (1973).
